nature-val-058.title: Use value: what a thing is good for
nature-val-058.text: Gold can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor. Each of those is a use, and together they make up its use value: the features that let a thing satisfy a human want or need. The idea comes from classical and Marxist economics. Adam Smith noticed that use and price can part company. Diamonds have little use but fetch a great deal in trade, while water is very useful yet cheap. For Marx, every commodity, a good made to be traded, is both a use value and an {{ref:nature-val-068}}: the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Not every useful thing can become a commodity. It must be tradable, its ownership must pass securely from one person to another, and there must be real demand. Later, marginalist economics traced use value to the {{ref:nature-econ-091}} consumers find in a good. Critics of turning nature into commodities still draw on Marx's double idea.

nature-val-068.title: Exchange value: what a thing trades for
nature-val-068.text: Marx gave every commodity four attributes: use value, exchange value, value and price. Exchange value is the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods. It is not the same as the money price, which only roughly matches it. Behind both, Marx held, lies value itself, set by the socially necessary labor time needed to produce a good: the work it typically takes. Modern neoclassical economics, the mainstream school, no longer treats exchange value as a separate idea. For it, exchange value is simply the market price, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-356}}. Before anything can be traded at all, certain conditions must hold: secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand. Critics of turning nature into commodities see a danger here. Expressing every kind of worth through a single exchange value puts very different things on one scale.

nature-val-065.title: Environmental philosophy: do rivers have rights?
nature-val-065.text: Do rivers have rights? Questions like that belong to environmental philosophy, the branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it. It emerged as a branch of its own in the 1970s. Its early figures include Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Richard Routley, Arne Næss and J. Baird Callicott. A major debate of the 1970s and 80s asked whether nature has value in itself or only as a means to human ends. On one side stood nature-centered views, including {{ref:nature-val-062}}; on the other stood human-centered ones. Another debate asks whether wilderness really exists, or whether, as William Cronon suggested, it is a cultural construct with colonial overtones. Today the field also takes up environmental activism, environmental justice, climate change and the depletion of finite resources.

nature-val-070.title: The paradox of value: why diamonds outprice water
nature-val-070.text: Nothing is more useful than water, Adam Smith observed, yet it will buy scarcely anything. Diamonds are far less useful and cost much more. This is the paradox of value, also called the diamond–water paradox. Smith is its classic presenter, though the puzzle appears as early as Plato's Euthydemus. Smith split 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', the ideas now called use value and exchange value, and noted that the most useful things often have little exchange value. Supporters of the labor theory of value had one answer: price reflects the toil of acquiring a good. Marginalists had another. They separated total utility from {{ref:nature-econ-091}}. Water is so plentiful that one more unit adds little, while scarce diamonds add more. Böhm-Bawerk's farmer with five sacks of grain shows the logic: he values the last sack by its least important use, feeding pigeons. Change the setting and the paradox flips. A person dying of thirst in a desert would pay more for water than for diamonds.

nature-val-057.title: Good as a means, or good in itself
nature-val-057.text: A hammer and a washing machine are valuable for what they do. Their value is instrumental: they are good as a means to an end. Happiness and pleasure are different. They are usually thought valuable for their own sake, the kind of worth explored in {{ref:nature-val-056}}. The sociologist Max Weber coined the terms. Not everyone accepts the split. John Dewey thought belief in value for its own sake was a mistake, and treated instrumental judgment as the only way to coordinate behavior well. J. Fagg Foster treated sustainability as a synonym for instrumental value, since success must never be short term.

nature-val-059.title: Anthropocentrism: putting humans at the center
nature-val-059.text: In 1906 J. Howard Moore argued that Darwin's theory of common descent had 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism. The idea has proved hard to kill. Anthropocentrism is the belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet. In this view humans stand apart from nature and above it, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use. Nature's value becomes instrumental: it matters as a means to human ends. {{ref:nature-val-037}} often treats this outlook as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere, the living envelope of the planet. Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism, the male-centered outlook, in feminist theory. Its defenders answer that the real problem is only shallow anthropocentrism. A sound long-term view, they argue, would keep the environment suitable for humans. William Grey called for an enriched idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views. Environmental philosophers still dispute who is right: whether human-centered thinking itself causes ecological harm, or only its shallow, short-term form. Religion enters the argument too. The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify the view, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation. Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks instead of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.

nature-val-056.title: Intrinsic value: worth for its own sake
nature-val-056.text: The Zoological Society of London warns that insect decline means a double loss. Species lose their instrumental value, and their intrinsic value as well. Intrinsic value, in ethics, is the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else. Instrumental value, by contrast, comes from a thing's relation to some other valued thing. Every major ethical theory treats something as intrinsically valuable. Virtue ethics points to flourishing; consequentialists, who judge acts by their results, point to pleasure. Some conservation biologists argue that nature has intrinsic value independent of its usefulness to people. Arne Næss's {{ref:nature-val-062}}, coined in 1972, gave all non-human beings this kind of worth. Whether absolute intrinsic value exists at all is debated. John Dewey accepted only value relative to a situation.

nature-val-062.title: Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness
nature-val-062.text: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, published in 1962, is often seen as the start of the movement. The Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss gave it a name, coining 'deep ecology' in 1972 and first using the phrase in a 1973 article. Deep ecology holds that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match. Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish. Næss set it against 'shallow ecology', which he criticized as utilitarian, human-centered and consumer-oriented. Deep ecology rejects nature as a resource to exploit. The materialist outlook, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced. Critics push back. Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores overconsumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic. Others call it Eurocentric or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge. Its ideas also feed arguments for valuing ecosystems outside markets.

nature-val-063.title: Ecocentrism: valuing nature as a whole
nature-val-063.text: Where anthropocentrism puts humans at the center, ecocentrism puts nature there. It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only, or the greater, bearers of intrinsic value. It values the biotic community, all the living things of a place, as a whole. Its aim is to keep the composition and processes of ecosystems intact, covering living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone. Aldo Leopold conceived the ethic, and his {{ref:nature-val-049}} is central to it. Supporters argue that a human-centered ethic always makes protecting nature depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives protection a firmer basis. Critics reply that it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

nature-val-060.title: Biocentrism: equal worth for every living thing
nature-val-060.text: The US Endangered Species Act has been described as unusually biocentric, because it puts non-human species first. Biocentrism is the environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things. It sits among close neighbors. Anthropocentrism is centered on humans. Sentientism values only beings that can feel pleasure or pain. Ecocentrism extends value to the whole of nature. Biocentrism rests on four pillars: humans and other species share Earth's community; all species depend on one another; each organism pursues its own good; and humans are not inherently superior. The family includes Albert Schweitzer's 'reverence for life', Peter Singer's animal liberation and Paul W. Taylor's biocentric egalitarianism. Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, rights for animals and environmental protection. Critics call it anti-human, and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.

nature-val-066.title: Three ways societies value nature
nature-val-066.text: Timber, clean water and air, carbon storage, pollination: these are the familiar ways nature serves people. They are only one of three kinds of value that societies see in the non-human world. The first kind is extrinsic, or instrumental, value: nature's usefulness to people, often called ecosystem services. Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value. That lets them enter impact assessments, {{ref:nature-val-001}} studies and national accounts. The second kind is intrinsic value. It holds that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans. The third kind, {{ref:nature-val-072}}, covers the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. IPBES, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

nature-val-064.title: Technocentrism: trusting science to fix nature
nature-val-064.text: Not everyone who worries about the environment wants to shrink industry. Technocentrism is a set of values centered on technology. It holds that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science. Technocentrics accept that environmental problems exist, but they do not see cutting industry as the solution. Ecocentrics, by contrast, see themselves as subject to nature. They prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.

nature-val-067.title: Social ecology: how people treat nature and each other
nature-val-067.text: 'The ecological crisis is a social crisis,' Murray Bookchin argued. His 1982 philosophy of social ecology links how humans treat nature to how they treat each other. Practices such as monocropping, growing a single crop over and over, and overfishing mirror social tendencies to dominate people. Bookchin defined nature itself as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom. Social ecology calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

nature-val-061.title: Rights of nature: writing nature's rights into law
nature-val-061.text: In 2008 Ecuador became the first country to put rights of nature in its constitution. Its Article 71 gives nature the right to respect for its existence and for the regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions and evolution. Rights of nature are the legal recognition that nature has rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law. The idea rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did. Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia have adopted such laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.

nature-val-073.title: Non-market goods: valuable but never sold
nature-val-073.text: Clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests share an awkward trait for economists. They are non-market goods, things that are not bought and sold in markets. Most environmental goods fall into this group. Without prices, putting a value on them is inherently uncertain. That difficulty is one reason environmental assets are usually left out of measures of wealth. In 1947 S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed a way around it: surveys asking people what such a good is worth to them, the approach later called {{ref:nature-val-085}}.

nature-val-069.title: Non-use value: caring about what you never use
nature-val-069.text: People can value a resource they have never used and never will. Economists call this non-use value. It is often attached to natural resources, and it stands apart from use value, which comes from using a good directly. Non-use value has several strands. It can include {{ref:nature-val-055}}, {{ref:nature-val-053}}, {{ref:nature-val-054}} and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it. All these categories grew from the first of them, introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964. Measuring them is hard. Market prices and other methods that read value from what people buy generally cannot capture it, because nobody is buying anything. Economists instead ask people directly in surveys, such as {{ref:nature-val-085}}. Attempts to value ecosystems sort the value of their services into use and non-use categories.

nature-val-052.title: Total economic value: adding up nature's worth
nature-val-052.text: Most people will never see a tiger in the wild, yet knowing tigers live there is worth something to many of them. Total economic value tries to count that, along with everything else. It is the full value people get from a natural resource, heritage site or piece of infrastructure, compared with not having it. In environmental economics it adds up the values an ecosystem provides. It is built in layers. Use value comes first, split into direct and indirect. Direct use covers removable products such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use covers non-removable things such as a sunset or a waterfall. Non-use value comes next. It covers simply knowing that a resource exists, as with those tigers. Two more strands look ahead. One, {{ref:nature-val-055}}, is placed on keeping the possibility of using a resource in future, even when that use is unlikely. Another, {{ref:nature-val-053}}, comes from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Adding the layers gives a single figure. {{ref:nature-val-001}} uses a similar approach.

nature-val-054.title: Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there
nature-val-054.text: A wilderness can be worth money even if nobody ever walks into it. That was John V. Krutilla's argument in his essay 'Conservation Reconsidered', which introduced the idea of existence value. It is the benefit people get simply from knowing that something exists, whether Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species. Because no direct use is needed, it is a leading example of non-use value. It is usually measured with {{ref:nature-val-085}} surveys. The idea has legal force. Since the case Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law. After the {{ref:nature-val-076}}, damages included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.

nature-val-055.title: Option value: paying to keep choices open
nature-val-055.text: Why fund a rail service or a wildlife refuge that most taxpayers will rarely use? Option value is one answer. It is what people are willing to pay to keep a public asset or service available, even if they are unlikely ever to use it. Policy assessments use it to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services. In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened natural resources so they might be used in future. Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964. He rested it on three conditions: future need is uncertain, loss would be irreversible or costly, and the asset cannot be stored. Later economists proposed refinements such as 'option price' and 'quasi option value', which stresses irreversibility. Option value in finance is a different idea, though both can be read as ways of valuing risk.

nature-val-053.title: Bequest value: saving nature for future generations
nature-val-053.text: Part of what people value in nature is what they can hand on. Bequest value is the satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Together with existence value, it makes up non-use value. It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service. Attempts to value ecosystems count it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations. In some optimization models, mathematical models that search for the best plan, it goes by another name: the 'salvage value' of the system.

nature-val-071.title: Direct and indirect use: taking versus enjoying
nature-val-071.text: Catching a fish and watching a waterfall both use nature, but only one takes something away. Direct use value comes from goods removed from nature, such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use value comes from benefits nature provides without anything being removed, such as a sunset or a waterfall. When ecosystems are valued, indirect use value arrives through the positive externalities ecosystems provide, benefits that reach people without a price. For livestock breeds, direct use is milk or meat. Indirect use includes regulating services such as nutrient cycling, seed dispersal and fire control. These values can often be inferred from behavior, such as recreational trip costs or house prices.

nature-val-072.title: Relational values: ties between people and nature
nature-val-072.text: Some ties to nature are neither about usefulness nor about worth in itself. Relational values arise from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. In one framing of nature's values they sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means. Ignoring them has costs. Western regenerative agriculture has been criticized for overlooking the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice: a wrong done to people in their capacity as knowers.

openers.val: Water keeps people alive, yet diamonds cost far more. That old puzzle opens this part of the course, which asks what it means to say nature has value. Economists separate a thing's usefulness from the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Philosophers ask a different question: is nature good only as a means to human ends, or good in itself? Between the belief that humans are the most important beings on the planet and the view that every living thing has equal worth lies a wide range of positions, and societies turn out to value the non-human world in several ways at once.
openers.kinds-of-value: Some things are very useful and trade for little; others are nearly useless and trade for a fortune. This chapter starts with that gap between usefulness and exchange. It then turns to philosophy, which separates what is good as a means from what is good as an end in itself. From there come rival views of humanity's place: one centered on people, one on all living things, one on nature as a whole, and one that trusts technology to solve environmental problems. Along the way the chapter sorts the ways societies see importance in the non-human world, as useful, as valuable in itself, and through relationships with it.

reviews.kinds-of-value: The chapter began with water and diamonds, a puzzle showing that usefulness and exchange value need not line up. Philosophy added a second split, between what is good as a means and what is good in itself, and anthropocentrism, biocentrism and ecocentrism each draw that line in a different place. Economists built their own ladder, from direct and indirect use through option, bequest and existence values, which together make up total economic value. Many of these values belong to non-market goods, so they must be estimated with surveys rather than read from sales. Relational values complete the picture: people also value nature through their ties to it.
